paras: The Springfield courthouse lynching was the hanging of five Black men on trial for the murder of farmer L. S. Laprade, seized from the sheriff by about 200 armed men at the courthouse in Springfield, Robertson County, Tennessee, on the night of February 18, 1881. The prisoners were taken just after the judge charged the jury, and the Tennessee Senate condemned it unanimously the next day. Governor Hawkins later offered a reward for the lynchers, first $500 and then $5,000.

Laprade lived alone near Sadlersville and was rumored to have inherited money; a party of Black men was accused of torturing and killing him in late summer 1880. Lynchers burned the feet of an old man, James Higgins, until he confessed, and on September 15 two other accused men, Bell and Jamison, were taken from the Springfield jail and lynched.

The remaining accused were brought from the Nashville jail for trial before Judge Joseph C. Stark on February 14, 1881, and that night about twenty-five mounted men broke open the jail office door. Stark and Attorney-General B. D. Bell talked them into leaving by promising a trial without a change of venue, and when the men asked whether they would be prosecuted, Stark said he "knew none of them, nor did he want to know any of them." Militia sent from Nashville was discharged the next day.

Two of the accused, Bill Murphy and Anthony Duffy, testified for the state and were released, and local reports blamed their release for reviving the demand for a lynching. On the evening of Friday, February 18, Judge Stark charged the jury at a night session.

As the sheriff started for the jail, about 200 men met him at the courtroom door with drawn pistols and took the five prisoners. They put out the lights and fired hundreds of shots into the air while the trial crowd jumped from the windows. The prisoners were hanged from ropes on the veranda over the east door; James Elder, who resisted, was thrown down and tied first. The Sun named the five as James Higgins, Lock Mallory, Lon Thiveat, Robert Thiveat and James Elder. After the men were dead the leader ordered, "Disperse, my men, to your homes," and the bodies hung until the next morning.

A coroner's inquest found death "by the hands of unknown persons," and the trial jury was dismissed without a verdict. The Tennessee Senate called on the governor to arrest and punish the lynchers. Governor Hawkins had offered $500 by early July and raised the reward to $5,000 on August 29, but no arrest or indictment appears in the coverage. A Springfield dispatch said public sentiment sustained the mob, and the Kentucky Gazette's reporter wrote that some "colored men" called it "too easy a death."

Nashville dispatches on the failed jail attack ran on February 15 and were reprinted in Richmond, Lancaster and New York. News of the lynching followed from February 19 under headlines such as the Sun's "One Murder and Eleven Lynchings" and the Richmond Dispatch's "Five Murderers Lynched," which misplaced the scene in "Winchester." Many accounts drew on the Nashville American's Springfield correspondent, who stressed that the mob was sober and disciplined and wrote that "the last seven were guilty and deserved their fate."

White papers called the prisoners "negroes" and "murderers" before any verdict and retold Laprade's torture at length; the Kentucky Gazette used a slur and called them "savages." The Clarksville Chronicle said Laprade's killers deserved lynching if anyone did, yet argued that "mob law is not a remedy for anything." The Highland News gave the story one line, and the Sacramento Record-Union cited the "seven negroes" as evidence that lynching victims in the South were nearly always Black.

A Nashville report of February 19 said Duffy and Murphy were found hanging near Guthrie, Kentucky, which would make seven dead. However, the Clarksville Chronicle said a week later that they had escaped, and the Hopkinsville South Kentuckian expected them to be lynched "if caught"; these later local reports are the stronger evidence.
Early accounts said Higgins had died in jail after a foot amputation, yet the Sun and the Nashville American's correspondent placed him among the hanged.

framing.detail: Nashville American correspondent described a sober, disciplined mob and wrote that the seven 'deserved their fate'.
Clarksville Chronicle editorial 'The Reign of Lawlessness' said the killers deserved lynching but mob law is no remedy.
Richmond Dispatch 'Five Murderers Lynched' and the Sun's 'One Murder and Eleven Lynchings' ran the wire with victims as 'negroes' and 'murderers'.
Kentucky Gazette 'Lively Times in Tennessee' used slurs and 'savages', dwelt on Laprade's torture, and praised the hanging as neater than a sheriff's.
Sacramento Record-Union editorial noted lynching victims were almost always Black and doubted Tennessee would act.
